pre.title: Before school: choose and register

note.title: Choose and register on time
note.text: Popular schools and concept schools (Montessori, Dalton, Jenaplan, Steiner, bilingual primaries) can have long local waiting lists, so check each school's registration rules early. Some schools keep their own early lists. Ask what such a list means at that school. In some cities there is a central procedure. In Amsterdam the municipality sends a letter and a form around the third birthday. You hand it in at your first-choice school by a deadline that depends on the birth date, and places follow priority rules and a lottery.

what: A child may start primary school at age 4. You can register from age 3, not earlier, and the Rijksoverheid asks you to register, if possible, at least 10 weeks before the fourth birthday. You may register at more than one school. Some municipalities have their own registration rules and deadlines. Many schools let a child come for a few settling-in days from age 3 years 10 months, up to 5 in total, but not every school offers them. Compulsory attendance starts on the first day of the month after the fifth birthday.

Public schools are open to every child, if they have a place. Schools can have a waiting list or priority rules. A denominational or other "special" school works from a religion or belief. Both kinds can follow methods such as Montessori or Dalton.
todo: Visit two or three schools and read their school guide.
Ask each school how sign-up, priority rules and any waiting list work.

g12.title: Year groups 1 and 2
what: The first two years of primary school, which has eight year groups. Most children start on their fourth birthday.
todo: Nothing to sign up for.
Ask how the school decides when a child moves on to year group 3. The school decides, together with you.

g35.title: Year groups 3 to 5
what: The school keeps a record of your child's progress. The school advice in year group 8 is the school's judgement of that whole record.
todo: Ask for a talk once a year, and ask early if you are worried.
If the school suggests repeating a year, ask for the reasons in writing (see Questions).

g67.title: Year groups 6 and 7
what: Many schools start talking with parents about a likely secondary level around now. The formal advice is only given in year group 8.
todo: Ask the teacher when your school starts the conversation.
Look at secondary schools and their open days. Dates differ per school.

g8.title: Year group 8: advice, test and sign-up
what: In year group 8 the school gives a school advice (schooladvies) and your child takes an end-of-primary test. The advice can name one level or two, for example havo and vwo. You sign up at a secondary school with the final advice. The advice is the starting point, not the final word. A secondary school may not place your child lower. It may choose to place your child higher, but that is not a right.
g8.checkedFor: Placement above or below the advice
g8.whatDated: Dates for school year 2026-27. They are set again every year.
g8.afterSignup: After the sign-up week, placements start from 1 April 2027, and the secondary school decides on admission by 12 May 2027. In some regions registration can open earlier, but only with a final advice, and it gives no advantage.

note2.title: The advice is not the final word
note2.text: The school advice is the starting point. Since the 2014-15 school year a secondary school must base admission on it, and in practice it places your child at least at that level. The main way up is the doorstroomtoets: if the result is higher than the advice, the primary school normally raises the advice, and it must explain why if it does not. Some secondary schools place a child above the advice, but the law gives you no right to this, so ask and explain why. Some schools start with a mixed first year, such as havo and vwo, which keeps options open. Moving up later is possible too. A vmbo-t (mavo) advice does not rule out vwo: a higher test result can raise the advice, a school may choose to place your child higher, or your child can stack levels (a vmbo-t diploma with one extra subject from the allowed list gives the right to havo 4, and a havo diploma the right to vwo 5). Even from vmbo, each step up has an official route, up to a PhD. People have done it. See the whole system page for the routes.

note.title: Act on time
note.text: Open days are usually in the winter, often January and February, and dates differ per school, so make a short list in the autumn. Cities such as Amsterdam, Utrecht and The Hague use central procedures with a lottery, so check your region's guide early and ask your child's school.

g8.whatUsual: The usual pattern: provisional advice in January, the test from late January into February, final advice in March, and sign-up at the end of March. The exact dates are set each year. For your child this is {label}.
todo: Visit open days and make a short list of schools that offer the advised level.
Ask how your region organises sign-up, and sign up within the sign-up week.
If you hope for a higher level than the advice, ask the school early whether it places children above the advice, and what it looks at.

A secondary school may refuse a child only on limited grounds, such as having no places left. It may not use extra tests or IQ scores to refuse a child. Bilingual (tto) and top-sport schools may test for their specific skills. A child who arrives from abroad has no Dutch advice, so the school looks at a doorstroomtoets if the child took one, and otherwise runs its own suitability check.

vo1.title: First year of secondary school (brugklas)
what: Year 1 usually lasts one year, sometimes two. Many schools combine at least two levels in one class, for example vmbo-t with havo, or havo with vwo. Some schools are single-level and start in one level directly.

vwo comes in two forms, atheneum and gymnasium. Both lead to the same vwo diploma level and to university admission. A gymnasium also teaches Latin and Greek. A categorical gymnasium is a school with only gymnasium classes. Some schools also offer a technasium or a bilingual (tto) stream.

Some schools offer the International Baccalaureate Middle Years Programme (MYP) in the lower years. It takes 5 years and ends in an MYP certificate. Ask the school how it fits with the Dutch levels and who can join.
todo: Ask how and when a child can move up or down a level. The school decides.
Ask what extra support the school gives.
Ask which vwo forms (atheneum, gymnasium), streams (tto, technasium) and IB programmes the school offers.

vo23.title: Years 2 and 3: choosing a pathway or profile
what: In vmbo, pupils choose a sector and one of four learning pathways by the end of year 2: basis (basisberoepsgerichte), kader (kaderberoepsgerichte), mixed (gemengde) or theoretical (theoretische). The pathways differ in level and in how practical or theoretical the lessons are. Basis leads to mbo level 2. Kader, mixed and theoretical lead to mbo level 3 or 4. A mixed or theoretical diploma plus one extra general exam subject also gives the right to start havo year 4.

In havo and vwo, pupils choose one of four profiles after year 3. Schools usually ask at the end of year 3. The profiles are culture and society (cultuur en maatschappij), economics and society (economie en maatschappij), nature and health (natuur en gezondheid) and nature and technology (natuur en techniek). Havo and vwo use the same four. Each profile points to different fields of study, so ask the school which studies each one opens.

After year 3 of havo or vwo, proof that you passed the first 3 years (the pass to year 4) gives access to mbo level 2, 3 or 4. This is a common route. A pupil who leaves in a later year (havo 4 or 5, vwo 4, 5 or 6) has passed those first 3 years too, so the same proof should work. Ask the mbo college which document it wants.
todo: Ask which profiles the school offers and which studies each one opens.
Moving between levels in these years is sometimes possible. The school decides.

fin.title: Exam year and what comes next
what: The final exam year is year 4 in vmbo (age 15 to 16), year 5 in havo (age 16 to 17) and year 6 in vwo (age 17 to 18). Practical education runs to about age 18.

In the final year, pupils sit national exams: in 6 subjects in vmbo, at least 7 in havo and at least 8 in vwo. Ask the school how much of each grade comes from the school's own tests and how much from the central exam.

In the last two years of secondary school, some schools offer the IB Diploma Programme (DP), and international schools teach it too. It takes 2 years. Joining is often linked to an international background, and the school decides. Ask how the IB fits with the Dutch exam at that school.
todo: For mbo, apply to the programme by 1 April of the exam year. You can apply later, but then you have no right to admission.
For hbo or wo, check the subjects and application dates of each programme early.
If your child may take the IB Diploma, ask the school who can join, what it costs and where the diploma leads.

he.title: After secondary school: mbo, hbo or wo
what: mbo (vocational college) has four levels: level 1 takes 1 year, level 2 takes 1 to 2, level 3 takes 2 to 3 and level 4 takes 3 to 4 years. Level 4 also has a one-year specialist programme that follows a level 3 or level 4 programme. Only a level 4 diploma gives the right to enter hbo. Level 1 (the entry programme) needs no diploma. It is for people who do not meet the level 2 requirements and for whom full-time compulsory schooling has ended, usually from about age 16. Levels 2, 3 and 4 need one of these: a vmbo diploma (any pathway for level 2, kader, mixed or theoretical for levels 3 and 4), proof that you passed the first 3 years of havo or vwo, or a havo or vwo diploma. Level 2 also accepts the entry programme diploma, and a college can exempt someone after an aptitude test. This is a common route from havo and vwo.

There are two ways to follow an mbo programme. BOL (school-based) has 20 to 60 percent practical training in a workplace. BBL (work-based) has at least 60 percent of the programme in a workplace. Both give the same diploma.

hbo (university of applied sciences, a hogeschool) is more practice-oriented than wo. It is taught in seven sectors: economics, healthcare, agriculture, pedagogical education (teacher training), socio-pedagogical education, arts and technology. A bachelor takes 4 years (sometimes 3 after vwo), and the first year is the first-year certificate (propedeuse). An associate degree takes 2 years. A master usually takes 1 year, sometimes 2.

wo (research university) is more theory- and research-oriented. It trains scientists, and professionals who apply scientific knowledge. A bachelor takes 3 years. A master takes 1 year in most fields, 2 years in technical, science and research masters, and 3 years in medicine, veterinary medicine, pharmacy and dentistry. A PhD (promotie) is not more school. In the Netherlands it is usually a paid research job at a university, and most PhD candidates are employees. It usually takes about 4 years. You can start one after a recognised master's degree, if a university offers you a place and a supervisor. A vwo diploma or a completed hbo first year (propedeuse) gives admission to a research university. A havo diploma does not give direct entry. Some programmes also ask for particular subjects, and some select applicants. An hbo bachelor usually needs a bridging programme (pre-master) before a wo master.

Numerus fixus and selection: some programmes admit only a fixed number of students. If more people apply than there are places, the institution may select. It can weigh the average final exam grade, motivation, personality and earlier school results. Check the rules and dates of each programme.

The IB Diploma (International Baccalaureate) can lead to hbo and wo too. Nuffic compares the full diploma with a vwo diploma. A university of applied sciences or a research university can still set subject and grade requirements, for example a maths level, so check each programme.

Without the usual diploma, people from age 21 can usually ask for an admission test. At hbo it is called the 21+ test (toelatingsonderzoek). Research universities (wo) use a similar entrance exam without the usual diploma, called colloquium doctum, often from age 21. Some sources use both names for either kind. The institution decides and runs it, and requirements differ.
todo: Check the entry rules, dates and any selection of each programme.
With an IB diploma, or without the usual diploma, ask the programme what it requires.

young.title: Newcomer class in primary school
young.what: Both exist: a special language class (schakelklas) for children who just arrived, and a regular class with extra Dutch lessons. Ask the school which it offers. A school board can open a temporary newcomer provision with the minister's permission. A child can be enrolled there for at most 2 years in total.

old.title: Newcomer class in secondary school (ISK)
old.what: A special class at a regular secondary school for recently arrived pupils who speak little or no Dutch. Lessons are mainly Dutch, plus other subjects that prepare pupils for regular classes and for regular secondary or mbo education. There is no official national length. Pupils move on to regular secondary school or mbo when the school decides they are ready.

todo: Ask your municipality, a reception location or the nearest school where places exist.
Places can be limited in some cities, so ask early.

path.pro: Practical education (praktijkonderwijs): pupils can stay until the end of the school year in which they turn 18, and the Inspectie can allow an extension. Admission needs a declaration of eligibility (toelaatbaarheidsverklaring) from the regional partnership (samenwerkingsverband), not only the school advice. Next: mbo. Once full-time compulsory schooling has ended, a pupil has a right to start the mbo entry programme (level 1, one year) without a vmbo diploma. Level 2 needs the entry programme diploma or another listed diploma, or an exemption after an aptitude test.
path.vbk: vmbo basis or kader: a diploma after 4 years. Basis leads to mbo level 2 (1 to 2 years). Kader leads to mbo level 3 (2 to 3 years) or level 4 (3 to 4 years), as the official entry requirements for 3 and 4 are the same. Programmes can add their own conditions, so ask the mbo college. A lower level is usually possible, and moving up later within mbo is possible.
path.vgt: vmbo gl/tl: a diploma after 4 years. Leads to mbo level 3 or 4. With one extra general exam subject, a diploma gives the right to enter havo year 4. This is a new school year, not a repeat. Without the extra subject, the havo school decides.
path.havo: havo: a diploma after 5 years. Leads to an hbo bachelor (4 years), an associate degree (2 years), mbo at any level (passing year 3 already gives access to mbo level 2, 3 or 4), or vwo year 5 (a havo diploma gives the right to enter, and it is a new school year, not a repeat). A havo diploma alone does not give access to wo.
path.vwo: vwo: a diploma after 6 years. Leads to a wo bachelor (3 years), an hbo bachelor or an associate degree. Passing year 3 already gives access to mbo level 2, 3 or 4. Some studies ask for particular subjects or select applicants.

pre.title: Choose and register at a primary school
pre.text: You can register from age 3 and, if possible, at least 10 weeks before the fourth birthday. Some municipalities, such as Amsterdam, have their own procedure and deadlines. Visit schools early and ask each how sign-up and any waiting list work.

early.text: Until then there is nothing to sign up for. Keep in touch with the teacher and ask early if you are worried about progress.

fin.title: Apply to the mbo programme
fin.text: For mbo, apply by 1 April of the exam year to keep the right to admission. For hbo or wo, each programme sets its own dates.

he.title: Check dates and entry rules

dates.d: The school gives a provisional advice. Ask for a talk and ask what it is based on.

Your child takes the test at school. If the test advice is higher than the provisional advice, the school adjusts the advice upward, unless it explains why that is not in your child's interest. If the result is more than half a level higher, the school may choose a level in between.
The school sets the final advice. Secondary schools admit on this advice and may not place your child lower. A higher placement is possible only if the school agrees, so ask.
Sign up at the secondary school you choose, with the final advice. Many regions allow more than one school, so check how yours works.

amsterdam.title: Amsterdam
amsterdam.text: Amsterdam runs a central lottery and matching procedure (centrale loting en matching) for secondary school. As we understand it, you rank schools that fit the school advice, each pupil gets a lot number, and places are matched using your ranking and the lot number. Do not assume the rules you know from another city apply here. The exact steps, the schools that take part and the dates change each year. Use the official Amsterdam sources and ask your child's school. Taking part is mandatory. How many schools you list depends on the advice. Pupils with a practical education advice do not take part in the lottery. Check the dates with OCO Amsterdam.

test.title: End-of-primary test (doorstroomtoets)
test.expl: In group 8 almost every child takes an end-of-primary test (doorstroomtoets). A few groups do not have to, for example children who have been in the Netherlands for four years or less and do not yet speak enough Dutch. Many parents still call it the Cito test. Schools choose from a list of approved tests, and the list changes by school year. For 2026-27 it has five: Dia, IEP, Leerling in beeld (Cito), Route 8 and the government's own DOE test. Each test has its own scale: an average of, for example, 177 on one test and 405 on another says nothing about which school did better. Compare a school's average only with the national average for the same test, shown below. The average is context for the school advice, not a grade for the school.
test.note: Compare averages only between schools that used the same test.

dist.title: How far pupils live
dist.expl: This is the straight-line distance between pupils' homes and the school, measured from the centre of the home postcode area. A small number means the school is mostly a neighbourhood school. A large number means pupils travel in from further away, which can matter for cycling and for friendships after school.

levels.title: Levels offered
levels.expl: Dutch secondary school has several levels. In vmbo there are four variants: basis and kader (more practical), and gl and tl (more theoretical). Then come havo (5 years) and vwo (6 years). A school can offer one level or several. A school with several levels under one roof makes it easier to move up or down later. The school decides on moving.

levels.atLeastNote: "At least" means DUO hides some small groups, so the real number is a little higher.

pass.title: Exam results
pass.explShort: The national exam happens in the last year of each level. Pass rates depend on who the school admits and on how many candidates there are.
pass.expl: In the final year of each level, pupils sit the national exam. The pass rate is the share of candidates who passed. It also depends on which pupils the school admits and, for small groups, on chance. It is not a ranking, and a high rate is not the same as a good fit for your child.

catch.title: Where pupils live
catch.expl: These are the postcode areas (the first four digits) most of the school's pupils come from. It shows how far the school draws. Open a postcode to see the route and the schools around it.

insp.title: Inspection
insp.expl: The Dutch Inspectorate of Education (Inspectie van het Onderwijs) judges the quality of schools. It publishes a judgement after an investigation, and many schools have none because they were not investigated recently. So having a judgement, or not having one, says little by itself. Many schools are listed without a current final judgement, and that is not a rating. We do not rank, sort or average schools by it.

od.expl: An open day lets you see the building, meet teachers and ask questions. Dates were collected from school websites and change every year, so treat them as a pointer and confirm with the school.
od.none: No upcoming open day found in our data.

sbo.title: About special primary schools
sbo.text: A special primary school (sbo) is for children who need more support than a regular school can give. Admission needs a formal decision first. Ask your child's current school or the samenwerkingsverband of your region.

so.title: Special education (SO and VSO)
so.expl: Special education has two parts. SO (speciaal onderwijs) is for children of primary-school age who need more support than a regular or special primary school (sbo) can give. VSO (voortgezet speciaal onderwijs) is the same for secondary-school age. Schools are grouped in four clusters by the kind of need they serve. A child can only be admitted after a formal decision. For clusters 3 and 4 it is a toelaatbaarheidsverklaring (TLV), which the samenwerkingsverband (the regional partnership of schools that arranges extra support) issues. For clusters 1 and 2 the institution decides whether a child qualifies. There are fewer of these schools than regular ones, so children often travel further.
so.noCount: Not shown (no count, or fewer than 5)
so.faqQ: How does my child get a place?
faqA: You cannot simply enrol your child. A formal decision comes first. For clusters 3 and 4 it is a toelaatbaarheidsverklaring (TLV), a formal statement that your child may attend special education.

The request is normally made together with the school your child attends now, with a description of your child's needs and of the support tried so far. The samenwerkingsverband of the region decides for clusters 3 and 4. If your child is not at a Dutch school yet, ask the school you have in mind, or the samenwerkingsverband of your area, where to start.

For clusters 1 and 2 the institution itself decides whether a child qualifies, so the route differs. A TLV is valid for one or more school years. Ask the school, and read the Rijksoverheid page on special education.

lj.title: Pupils per year group
lj.note: Groups 1 and 2 are the youngest children (about 4 to 6 years). Group 8 is the last year before secondary school.

rn.title: Reading, language and maths levels
rn.expl: At the end of primary school the doorstroomtoets checks pupils against national reference levels. 1F is the fundamental level: the basics that every pupil should have by the end of primary school. 2F (reading and language) and 1S (maths) are the higher target level. National policy expects the basic level from every pupil and the higher level from a smaller group, the stronger pupils. So a school with fewer pupils at 2F or 1S than at 1F is normal. The share at the higher level depends a lot on who the school admits.
rn.small: Small group: the percentages can swing a lot.
rn.note: Each bar is the share of tested pupils at that level or higher. A subject is left out when DUO hides a group of fewer than 5 pupils.
rn.src: Source: DUO, pupils per reference level for language and maths

hv.title: Advice reconsidered after the test
hv.expl: After the doorstroomtoets, a school must look again at its advice if the test result points to a higher level than the advice. This is called reconsideration (heroverweging). After the test the advice can only go up, never down. Reconsidering does not always change the advice: the school may keep it if it explains why that is in the child's interest, and a practical education (praktijkonderwijs) advice is not raised when the test points to practical education or vmbo-bb.
hv.line: Advice reconsidered for {rec} leavers, raised for {rai}.
hv.of: Out of {n} group 8 leavers who took the test.
hv.noRatio: The two counts are shown separately and should not be turned into a percentage, because they may not cover exactly the same pupils.
hv.src: Source: DUO, reconsiderations and adjusted advice

ce.title: Exam grades
ce.expl: Each exam grade is on the Dutch scale of 1 to 10. The central exam (centraal examen) is the national part of the final exam. The school exam (schoolexamen) is set and marked by the school during the last years. The final list (cijferlijst) is the average of the final grades of all subjects. The tables show the mean grade of the candidates per level and exam year. The means also reflect which pupils the school admits.
ce.caption: Exam grades {level}
ce.partialNote: * Some small groups are left out of this figure.
ce.note: Each figure is approximate: it is the candidate-weighted average of the means DUO publishes per programme or profile. Groups with fewer than 5 candidates are left out. The school exam and final list grades are kept for the last three exam years. A dash means there is no figure for that year.

zb.title: Repeaters and moves between levels
zb.expl: Some pupils repeat a year (zittenblijvers). Others move to a lower level (afstromers) or to a higher level (opstromers). Some movement is normal, especially in the first years, while the school confirms which level fits. The numbers do not say why pupils move, so use them as a question for the school.
zb.note: All levels together, for this location. DUO hides most counts below 5.
zb.src: Source: DUO, repeaters and up- and down-streaming in secondary education

ov.title: Inspectie results (calculated)
ov.expl: Every year the Inspectie calculates three result measures for each type of secondary education at a location, from three years of data. They are compared with a norm that is corrected for the pupil population. This is not a judgement after a school visit, and not a ranking.

def.ob: The share of pupils who get through the first years (onderbouw) on time, without delay.
def.bb: The share of pupils from year 3 who progress without delay: they move up, pass the exam or move to a higher level, as the Inspectie calculates it.
def.ce: The mean central-exam grade of the candidates, on the scale of 1 to 10.
def.verdict: A verdict the Inspectie derives from the three measures for this type of education: sufficient, insufficient, or insufficient unless a closer look shows otherwise. It is a calculation, not a judgement of the school.

ov.caption: Inspectie results {level}
ov.note: Norms are corrected for the pupil population, so they differ between schools. Being below a norm on one measure does not make a school weak. Ask the school about it. We do not rank or colour schools by these numbers.
ov.src: Source: Inspectie van het Onderwijs, onderwijsresultaten voortgezet onderwijs 2026 (CC0), three-year averages

op.title: Placement compared with the primary advice
op.expl: In year 3 the Inspectie compares the level each pupil is in with the level the primary school advised. The measure is the share of pupils placed above their advice minus the share placed below it, in percentage points. It is calculated for the whole location, for pupils who started there in year 1.
op.note: Compare the result with the norm only. This norm is not corrected for the pupil population: the Inspectie compares schools with the same offer. A higher number means more pupils were placed above their advice relative to those placed below it.

tj.note: Year 1 is the first year of secondary school. A number with a plus sign is at least that many, because DUO hides small groups. 0 means no pupils in that year.
tj.caption: Pupils per school year and level

pf.title: Profile choice in the upper years
pf.expl: In the upper years of havo (years 4 and 5) and vwo (years 4 to 6) pupils choose a profile, a package of subjects that fits a field of study. The table counts the pupils in each profile per year. It shows which profiles the school offers and how many pupils pick each one. It does not say which profile is better.

contact.title: School board and contact
contact.expl: The board (bevoegd gezag) is the organisation that runs the school and is legally responsible for it. One board can run many schools. Each school also belongs to a samenwerkingsverband (SWV), the regional partnership of schools that arranges extra support for pupils who need it.
contact.swvNote: Pupils who need more support than the school can give get it through the SWV. Ask the school which SWV it belongs to and how a support request works.
contact.swvDerived: The open data does not list the SWV per VSO school. This one is the SWV that all secondary schools in the same municipality belong to, so it can differ from the school's own SWV.
contact.swvNoName: The open files only give a code for this SWV, not its name.
contact.boardNote: The telephone number is the school's published contact number. The number of locations counts the schools of this board that are in this data (primary, special and secondary).

us.title: Leaving profile of VSO pupils in this region
us.note: This is regional, not about this school. It counts all VSO pupils in the samenwerkingsverband by the leaving profile they follow, which is the route each pupil is prepared for. Counts under 5 are hidden. School year 2025 to 2026.

staff.title: Staff at school group level
staff.expl: This shows how many people work for the school group this location belongs to, counted in full-time equivalents (FTE). Two part-time staff members of half a week each count as 1 FTE. The pupils per teacher figure divides the pupils by the teaching staff in FTE.
staff.group: Whole school group (all locations with the same BRIN4 code), October {y}.
staff.note: These are figures for the whole group, not for this location. They are not a measure of class size: the numbers also include teachers who do not teach a class, such as remedial teachers.

hol.title: School holidays
hol.expl: The Netherlands has three holiday regions (north, middle and south). The summer holiday starts on a different date in each region. Regions also differ in some of the other holidays.
hol.region: This school is in holiday region {region}.
hol.caption: School holidays {y}
hol.note: The Christmas, May and summer holidays are fixed. The autumn and spring dates are advice, and a school can choose other dates once its participation council agrees. Check the school's own calendar.
hol.src: Source: Rijksoverheid school holiday dates (open data), region from the DUO address file

lr.title: Results compared with the Inspectie signal value
lr.expl: At the end of primary school the doorstroomtoets shows whether pupils reach set levels in reading, language and maths. The Inspectie pools three years (2024, 2025 and 2026) and compares the share of pupils who reach a level with a signal value (signaleringswaarde). The signal value for the higher level (2F and 1S) is lower for schools whose pupils have more disadvantages (see the schoolweging below).
lr.d1f: The basic level (fundamentaal niveau). Almost every pupil is expected to reach it.
lr.d2f: The higher level: 2F for reading and language, 1S for maths. It is a stretch level, so the signal value is much lower.

o.small: Small school: judged over five years, so no outcome here
o.few: Too little data for an outcome

lr.n: Based on {n} pupils over three years.
lr.small: This is a small number, so the percentages can swing a lot.
lr.note: Below the signal value is a reason for the Inspectie to look closer, not a verdict on its own. The figures are for the school unit the Inspectie uses, which can cover more than one location. This is context, not a ranking.

sw.title: Schoolweging
sw.ctx: The average across Dutch primary school locations is {mean} (middle value {median}).
sw.expl: The schoolweging is a number that Statistics Netherlands (CBS) calculates for each primary school. It describes how complex the pupil population is, based on the education of the parents and the average education of the mothers at the school, the parents' country of birth, how long the mother has lived in the Netherlands and whether the parents are in debt restructuring. The scale runs from about 20 to 40. A higher number means more pupils with such disadvantages. It is an average of 2022/23 to 2024/25. The Inspectie uses it to set the signal value above.

sv.title: Suspensions and removals
sv.expl: Secondary schools must tell the Inspectie when a pupil is suspended for more than one day, or removed from the school. Primary and special schools must report suspensions of more than one day. This shows the number reported for the school year 2025 to 2026 (1 August 2025 to 31 July 2026). It is a count, not a rate: a bigger school has more pupils. It says little on its own.
sv.susp: Suspensions of more than one day
sv.none: The Inspectie file for 2025 to 2026 lists no suspensions or removals for this school.
sv.unitVo: The count is for this location. It adds up the education types the Inspectie lists for it.
sv.unitOne: The count is for the school unit the Inspectie uses, which here is this location.
sv.unitMany: The count is for the school unit the Inspectie uses, which covers {n} locations. It is not split per location.
sv.small: A very small number can be a single pupil or a single event.
sv.note: Only cases that schools reported to the Inspectie are counted. Primary and special schools report suspensions only. The data does not say why.
sv.src: Source: Inspectie van het Onderwijs, schorsingen en verwijderingen 2025 to 2026 (CC0)

ex.title: Excellent school predicaat
ex.expl: The Inspectie used to give the predicaat Excellent School to schools with outstanding results in a field of their own choice. It was awarded for three years.
ex.line: This school was on the Inspectie list of excellent schools until 1 July {y} (round {rng}).

adviceNote.title: The advice is not the final word
adviceNote.text: The school advice is the starting point. Since the 2014-15 school year a secondary school must base admission on it, and in practice it places your child at least at that level. The main way up is the doorstroomtoets: if the result is higher than the advice, the primary school normally raises the advice, and it must explain why if it does not. Some secondary schools place a child above the advice, but the law gives you no right to this, so ask and explain why. Some schools start with a mixed first year, such as havo and vwo, which keeps options open. Moving up later is possible too: see Other ways through below.
adviceNote.text2: A vmbo-t (mavo) advice does not rule out vwo. A higher doorstroomtoets result can raise the advice, or a school may choose to place your child higher. Or your child stacks the levels: a vmbo-t diploma with one extra subject from the allowed list gives the right to havo 4, and a havo diploma gives the right to vwo 5. Even from vmbo, each step up has an official route: mbo level 4, hbo bachelor, a pre-master, a wo master, then a PhD. People have done it.

realRoutes.title: Real routes: reader experiences
realRoutes.one: A reader went from vmbo to a PhD.
realRoutes.two: Another got a vmbo-t (mavo) advice in 2008 and started in a vwo first year. Before 2014 that was allowed: a secondary school made its own admission decision, and some used the Cito score or their own entrance test. Today admission must be based on the advice, and the usual way up is a higher doorstroomtoets result.
realRoutes.note: These are experiences readers shared. They are not rules or sourced facts, and every child's route depends on the child and the school.

faq.heading: Questions parents ask
faq.intro: Short answers to what parents new to the Netherlands ask about Dutch schools. Each answer lists its sources.

items.q: When must my child go to school?

blocks.p: A child may start at age 4. School is compulsory (leerplicht) from the first day of the month after the fifth birthday. It applies to every child who lives in the Netherlands, whatever the nationality.

Compulsory attendance ends at the end of the school year in which the child has been at school for 12 full school years, or at the latest at the end of the school year in which the child turns 16 (Leerplichtwet, article 3). After that, young people without a havo, vwo or mbo level 2 diploma must keep studying until they are 18 (kwalificatieplicht). This does not apply to young people who followed practical education (praktijkonderwijs) or certain tracks of special secondary education (vso).

If you live in the Netherlands but your child goes to a school abroad, for example in Belgium or Germany, you can ask your municipality's truancy officer for an exemption. You then report every year that your child attends school abroad.

items.q: Which year group will my child join?

blocks.p: Not by a national rule. The old rule that a child joins group 3 depending on a 1 October birthday ended in 1985. Some schools still use a similar guide.

Today the school decides, together with you, and looks at age, development and earlier schooling. Children usually start in group 1 around the age of four and are in group 8 at about age 11. For a child who arrives from abroad, the school decides which year fits.
Ask how the school makes this decision, and what extra help your child gets for Dutch. The decision to move up or repeat a year is also the school's.

items.q: We arrive in the middle of the school year. Can my child still start?

blocks.p: Yes. If you move house, you can register your child at a secondary school at any time of the year. For primary school you can register your child in writing; ask the school how it handles a start in the middle of the year.

The school may have no places or a waiting list, so register at more than one school if you can. Bring an identity document or birth certificate and, if your child went to school before, proof of de-registration from the previous school. Ask the school whether it also wants school reports. If your child has no citizen service number (BSN) yet, the school can use a temporary education number.

A place in a newcomer class can take time; ask the school how long, because this differs per school. For children who need extra support, the rule is to register in writing, if possible at least 10 weeks before the date you want your child to start. If you arrive in the middle of the year, register as early as you can and say at once that your child needs support. The school then has 6 weeks to decide, and can extend this once by up to 4 weeks. If there is no decision after 10 weeks and your child is not at another school, your child gets a temporary place.

items.q: Do I need a BSN or an address before I can register?

blocks.p: You can register your child without a citizen service number (BSN). You register your child yourself, and the school asks for the BSN. If your child has none yet, the school can enrol your child with a temporary education number (onderwijsnummer), which DUO issues. Tell the school when your child gets a BSN.

If you will live in the Netherlands for more than 4 months, you register at your municipality (the population register, BRP) within 5 days of arrival, and you get a BSN. Children who come with you must come to the town hall too. For a stay of less than 4 months you can register in the non-residents register (RNI) and still get a BSN. Ask the municipality which documents it needs; we did not find a national list.

Ask the school what it needs, and start early. We found no national rule that you need a home address to register your child at a school, so ask the school. We could not confirm that the Amsterdam central procedure asks for proof of a future address, so ask the municipality.

items.q: Can my child join a Dutch school without speaking Dutch?

blocks.p: Yes. What is on offer depends on age. In primary school, newcomers can join a language class or a transition class (taalklas or schakelklas), or a regular class with extra Dutch lessons.

In secondary school, pupils from age 12 who recently arrived and speak little or no Dutch can join an international transition class (ISK). Pupils learn Dutch and prepare for regular secondary school or mbo. There is no official national length. Two years is the limit for the extra funding, not a standard stay.
Places can be limited, so ask early. Ask your municipality, the reception site or a nearby school where places exist.

Schools get extra funding for a newcomer in the first two years. School is compulsory for every child aged 5 to 16 who lives in the Netherlands, whatever the nationality, so a place must be found even without Dutch. From 16 to 18 a young person without a havo, vwo or mbo level 2 diploma must keep going to school.

items.q: Is repeating a year normal, and who decides?

blocks.p: The school decides whether a child moves up or repeats a year. The law does not say when a child must repeat a year. The school guide describes how each school handles it. The school must tell you if your child repeats a year. If you disagree, you can object through the school's complaints procedure.

ul: Ask for the reasons in writing: which results and observations, and which support has been tried.
Ask for a meeting with the teacher and the school's learning-support coordinator (intern begeleider).
Repeating is not automatically good or bad. Ask the school what it expects to change.
If language is the issue, ask what support exists. Repeating a year may not fix a speech or pronunciation question, so ask the school and, if needed, a speech therapist.

blocks.p: We have no official figure for how common it is, so we do not give one.

items.q: Can I choose any primary school?

blocks.p: You can register at any school, and at more than one. There is no national catchment area. A school can be full, have a waiting list, or give priority to certain children.

Some municipalities have a central procedure. In Amsterdam, for example, priority goes first to a brother or sister already at the school, then to children from a linked playgroup, children of staff and children who live close by. A lottery decides when there are more applicants than places.
The school's admission policy is public, usually in the school guide or on its website. A public school is open to every child. Ask each school how it handles registration and waiting lists.

items.q: Can a religious school refuse my child?

blocks.p: A public school is open to every child, and its lessons are not based on a religion. A bijzondere (special) school teaches from a religion, a belief or a view on education. A school with a religious basis may ask parents to respect that basis, or to sign a statement that they subscribe to it, and may set religious requirements for teachers.
This applies only where it relates to the school's foundation. A school may not discriminate, for example on origin. A court decides in a dispute.
Read the school guide and ask about the admission policy before you register.

items.q: Can I choose any secondary school? Is there a catchment area?

blocks.p: You can register at any secondary school that offers the advised level. You may register at more than one, because a school can be full. A school may refuse a child only on limited grounds, such as having no places left. A school may also place your child above the advice if it agrees, but it does not have to.

It may not use extra tests or IQ scores. A bilingual (tto) or top-sport school may test only for its special skills. Some regions have agreements between schools on how pupils are spread, and places can be given by lottery.
Rules differ per region. Registration is usually in the sign-up week at the end of March. Ask your child's primary school how your region works.

items.q: Which cities use a lottery for secondary school?

blocks.p: Where a school has more applicants than places, a lottery can be used. Several large regions do, and the rules differ. Amsterdam places pupils for regular secondary schools in one central round. A computer gives each pupil a random lot number and places pupils, in lot order, at the highest school on their ranked list that still has room. A pupil who registers late or withdraws can join a second round. To get a place at a regular Amsterdam secondary school you register online in the central registration week.

In Amsterdam the number of schools on the list depends on the advice: 12 for havo and vwo, 6 for vmbo-gl/tl, and 4 for vmbo-b and vmbo-k (for entry in 2027). A complete list gives a placement guarantee at one of the listed schools. Pupils for practical education, special secondary education (VSO), the Kopklas, the ISK and the intermediate provision do not take part in the lottery and register another way. A child from abroad without a Dutch advice registers with the first-choice school before the central week.

In the four Utrecht regions (Utrecht and Stichtse Vecht, Utrecht West, Zuid-Utrecht and Zuidoost Utrecht) a lottery is held at schools that have more first-choice applications than places. In 2026 this happened at twelve schools.

In Haaglanden eight schools drew lots in 2026, and pupils who were not drawn go into a central lottery for a place at another school on their list. Rotterdam and Eindhoven have their own regional procedures; we could not confirm the details from an official page, so read the current guide of your region. We could not confirm the rules for Haarlem or Nijmegen either.
Procedures can change every year, so read the current guide of your region and ask your child's primary school.

items.q: How does the school advice work, and can I change it?

blocks.p: The school decides the advice. At the end of group 8 the school gives a school advice (schooladvies), based on your child's whole record. It can name one level or two, for example havo and vwo. In January the school gives a provisional advice.

Your child then takes the end-of-primary test. If the test advice is higher, the school adjusts the advice upward, unless it decides this is not in your child's interest, and then it must explain why. If the test result is more than half a level higher, the school may choose a level in between. The test cannot lower the advice.

The school gives the final advice by 24 March 2027. A secondary school must place your child at least at the advised level, unless you explicitly ask for a lower level, and may not require a one-level advice.

The advice is the starting point, not the final word. A secondary school may not place your child below it, unless you explicitly ask for a lower level. It may place your child above it, but that is not a right. The school decides, so talk to the school and explain why you think your child can do it. Some schools have a mixed first year, such as havo and vwo, which can keep options open, depending on the school's rules for moving up. A child with a double advice can always be registered for the higher of the two levels, if the school offers that level. The school chooses the first-year class, and a school that offers only one level does not have to take a child with a double advice. A child can also still move up later. See Other ways through on the whole system page.

items.q: How do I ask the school about the advice, or ask for a second opinion?

blocks.p: The school advice is the school's professional judgement of your child's whole record. The end-of-primary test can raise it, and the school must explain if it does not raise it. Secondary schools admit on the final advice, and they may not ask a primary school to give an advice for one level only.

blocks.say: Could we meet to talk about the advice? Which results and observations is it based on? What would change it?

ul: Ask for the final advice and the reasons in writing.
Ask whether the learning-support coordinator can join the meeting.
Independent assessments exist, for example from a child psychologist or an assessment bureau. Costs and insurance cover vary a lot, so ask before you book.
The advice is a starting point. Secondary schools may not place your child lower. Ask the schools you like whether they ever place children above the advice, and what they look at.

items.q: My child got a vmbo advice, what now?

blocks.p: vmbo takes 4 years and is a full route, not a dead end. After it comes mbo. The pathway matters: basis leads to mbo level 2, while kader, mixed or theoretical (gl/tl) lead to level 3 or 4. An mbo level 4 diploma gives the right to enter hbo, and a completed first hbo year (propedeuse) gives admission to a research university, subject to programme requirements. That route takes more years than going straight through vwo, but every step exists.

ul: Ask which pathway the advice means: basis, kader or gl/tl.
Consider a school with several levels under one roof, and ask how placing and moving between levels works there. The school list shows which levels each school offers.
After vmbo gl/tl, a diploma with one extra general subject gives the right to join havo. Without it, the havo school decides.

The advice is the school's judgement. The end-of-primary test can raise it, and the school must explain if it keeps a lower one. A secondary school may place your child higher if it agrees, so ask. Moving up later is also possible.

items.q: What are atheneum and gymnasium within vwo?

blocks.p: vwo takes 6 years and prepares for study at a research university. It comes in two forms: atheneum and gymnasium. Both take the same vwo final exam, and both lead to the same vwo diploma level and the same university admission. The diploma says which form the pupil followed.

ul: A gymnasium also teaches Latin and Greek.
A categorical gymnasium is a school with only gymnasium classes. A categorical gymnasium may also enrol atheneum pupils if it offers atheneum and says so in its name.
Some schools offer a technasium stream (design and research assignments for outside clients) or a bilingual (tto) stream. Not every school has them.

blocks.p: The choice between atheneum and gymnasium does not change what the vwo diploma opens. Some university programmes still ask for particular subjects, whichever form a pupil followed.

blocks.say: Ask which forms and streams the school offers, and whether a pupil can change between atheneum and gymnasium. The school decides.

items.q: What is the difference between a Dutch school, an international school and a bilingual school?

blocks.p: A Dutch school teaches in Dutch and follows the Dutch curriculum. It is paid for by the state, and there are no tuition fees. An international school teaches in English or another language and may follow an international programme such as the IB.

Dutch International Schools are government funded and meant for children of internationally mobile families. Fully private international schools set their own fees. A bilingual school (tto) is a Dutch secondary school where at least half of the lessons in the first years of havo and vwo (30 percent in vmbo) are taught in another language, usually English. Pupils take the normal Dutch exams and also get an extra bilingual certificate.

Your choice depends on how long you will stay, your child's age and which language your child needs later. Bilingual primary education (tpo) also exists: Nuffic says children get 30 to 50 percent of the teaching time in English, German or French. It started as a government pilot (the evaluation was published by the Rijksoverheid in 2023), so ask whether a school near you offers it. For secondary school the Rijksoverheid says the other language is usually English, and Nuffic names English.

items.q: Can my child take the International Baccalaureate (IB) in the Netherlands?

blocks.p: At some schools, yes. The IB is an international programme with its own diploma. International schools teach it, and some Dutch secondary schools may offer it too (our school list has an IB filter; confirm with the school). The IB calls approved schools IB World Schools, and some offer every phase while others offer only one or two.

ul: Lower years: the Middle Years Programme (MYP) takes 5 years and ends in an MYP certificate. Nuffic compares it with 4 years of vwo.

Last two years: the Diploma Programme (DP) takes 2 years. Nuffic lists the MYP certificate as the entry requirement, but schools set their own rules. The Dutch International Secondary Schools, for example, ask for a havo diploma or a pass into vwo year 5, plus enough English.

Who can join: this is often linked to an international background, and the school decides. The funded Dutch International Schools (DIS) admit a pupil under national rules, for example a non-Dutch pupil whose parent works in the Netherlands for a limited time, or a Dutch pupil who lived abroad because of a parent's posting and went to school there for more than two years (the law for primary departments says more than two years; the DIS page says at least two).

Cost: a funded school may ask a parental contribution, and the minister wrote in 2023 that funded international education may make it compulsory. Amounts differ per school, so ask for the fee schedule.

blocks.p: Where it leads: Nuffic compares the full IB Diploma with a vwo diploma and says it gives access to higher education. A university of applied sciences or a research university can still set subject and grade requirements. TU Delft, for example, accepts only Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at higher level. Check each programme.

blocks.say: Ask the school which IB programmes it runs, whether it is an IB World School, who can join, what it costs and how the IB fits with the Dutch levels.

items.q: What do international schools cost?

blocks.p: Dutch schools funded by the state do not charge tuition. International schools do. Private international schools set their own fees.
The amounts below are rough estimates, not prices. Fees differ per school and change every year. Always check the school's own fee schedule before you decide.

Private international schools: for 2026-27, one Amsterdam school (ISA) publishes tuition from about 22,800 euro a year in nursery to about 32,800 euro in the last two years. ISA's fee page lists tuition only. Some schools add a registration fee or a deposit, so ask what comes on top.

Dutch International Schools are government funded and set their fees per school. One example: International School Eindhoven lists, for 2026-27, 6,690 euro a year in its primary international department and 8,569 to 9,466 euro in secondary, plus a registration fee of 200 euro. A funded international department may make the parental contribution compulsory (Kamerstuk 22452 nr 88).

blocks.say: Ask each school for its current fee schedule, what extra costs come on top, and the rules on who can apply.

items.q: I have the 30% ruling. Does that change school choice?

blocks.p: It can matter for international school fees, but not for state-funded Dutch schools, which charge no tuition. Employers can pay school fees for an international school tax-free as extraterritorial costs. The rule is in the Wet op de loonbelasting 1964 (article 31a, paragraph 2, under e) and the Uitvoeringsbesluit loonbelasting 1965 (articles 10e and 10ea). The Belastingdienst conditions include the type of school (an international school or international department, with education based on a foreign system) and who it is meant for (mainly children of seconded employees). This site gives no tax advice.

From 1 January 2027 the tax-free allowance under the 30% ruling falls to 27%. This is law: it was adopted with the Belastingplan 2025, which the Eerste Kamer approved on 17 December 2024. The transitional rules depend on when your ruling started. If it started up to 31 December 2023, you keep 30% and the current salary norm. If it started in 2024, you move to 27% in 2027 under the current salary norm. If it started from 1 January 2025, you move to 27% in 2027 and a higher salary norm applies. In 2025 and 2026 the maximum is 30%. Since 2026 the allowance is calculated on a salary of at most EUR 262,000 a year (at most EUR 78,600 at 30%).

School fees for an international school are a separate tax-free item. They come on top of the 30% (Wet op de loonbelasting 1964, article 31a, paragraph 8; Uitvoeringsbesluit loonbelasting 1965, article 10ea), and the change to 27% only replaces the 30% and leaves the school fees alone (Kamerstuk 36602 nr 41). Without the ruling, school fees can be reimbursed tax-free as actual extraterritorial costs only if the employer can show a link with the temporary stay outside your home country. In general there is no such link if the child already attended that school before the posting (Belastingdienst, KG:041:2023:12).
Do not choose a school only because of a tax rule. Ask your employer's HR or a tax adviser before you sign a contract with a school, and read the current Belastingdienst pages.

items.q: Will my child's foreign school diplomas be recognised?

blocks.p: For study in the Netherlands, Nuffic compares a foreign diploma with a Dutch one. This is called a credential evaluation. It covers higher education and almost all secondary diplomas.

It is not binding. Dutch universities and universities of applied sciences decide who they admit, and they can add their own requirements, such as subjects or a language test. Ask the programme you want before you pay for an evaluation.
For school places, ask the school what documents it wants. Keep copies of reports and diplomas, with translations if needed.

items.q: Is Dutch school free? What is the ouderbijdrage?

blocks.p: State-funded schools do not charge tuition. Schools may ask for a voluntary parental contribution (ouderbijdrage) for extras such as trips, sports days or celebrations. You do not have to explain why you do not pay. The parent members of the participation council (MR) must agree with the amount. The voluntary rule does not apply to international schools that are aimed at expats, where the contribution can be compulsory (see the answer on international school costs).

Since a law that took effect on 1 August 2021, a school may not exclude your child from activities because you did not pay, and may not give your child a free replacement activity instead (Kamerstuk 35063 nr 15). The school guide must say that the contribution is voluntary and that not paying does not lead to exclusion (Wet op het primair onderwijs, article 13, paragraph 1 e). Lunch supervision (overblijven) costs extra: the school sets the amount and the participation council must approve it.

If a school asks you to pay as if it were compulsory, point to the school guide and the Rijksoverheid information. You can also contact the parent members of the participation council (MR), Ouders & Onderwijs (088 605 0101, free) or the Inspectie (088 669 6060, weekdays 9.00 to 16.30).

items.q: What are school hours and what happens at lunch?

blocks.p: Hours differ per school. Some primary schools have a continuous schedule (continurooster): all children stay at school during lunch, teachers supervise, and parents do not pay a lunch fee, although a voluntary contribution can be requested. Other schools have a break at midday.

Then children go home or stay for lunch supervision (overblijven or tussenschoolse opvang, TSO). The school must organise this on request, and parents pay a contribution. The parent council must agree with the amount.
Check the school guide for the weekly schedule, the lunch rules and the cost.

items.q: What about after-school care and childcare benefit?

blocks.p: After-school care (BSO) is separate from school. A BSO provider collects children from school and keeps them until parents finish work. You pay the provider.

The state can pay part of the cost through the childcare benefit (kinderopvangtoeslag), paid by Dienst Toeslagen. In 2026 the maximum hourly rate for BSO is 9.98 euro and the maximum benefit is 96 percent for lower incomes. The percentage falls as income rises.

The rules change from year to year, and conditions apply to your work, income and residence. Lunch supervision at school (TSO) does not count as childcare for the benefit. Check the current rules at Dienst Toeslagen before you sign a contract.

items.q: Can we take a holiday outside the school holidays?

blocks.p: Normally no, once your child is subject to compulsory education. The school head can give extra leave only if the nature of your work means you cannot take a family holiday in any school holiday, for example seasonal work. It is for up to 10 days, once per school year.
For this work-related leave, apply at least 8 weeks before the trip. It is not possible in the first two weeks of the school year. If you take your child out without permission, you can be fined.

The Rijksoverheid does not give an amount, so ask your municipality's truancy officer. A child of 4 is not yet subject to compulsory attendance, but ask the school what it expects. Longer absences are not allowed under this rule.

items.q: My child needs extra support. What are my rights?

blocks.p: Dutch schools have a duty of care (zorgplicht). The school where you register your child must offer a suitable place, in the school itself or at another school. Schools work together in regional partnerships (samenwerkingsverbanden passend onderwijs).

Register in writing at least 10 weeks before the new school year and tell the school about the support your child needs. The school has 6 weeks to decide and can extend this once by up to 4 weeks. If you disagree with the plan, you can involve your regional partnership.
Special primary schools (sbo) and special schools need a formal declaration of eligibility (toelaatbaarheidsverklaring) first. A practical education (praktijkonderwijs) advice needs one too.

items.q: What does "university" mean here (wo vs hbo)?

blocks.p: Dutch higher education has two kinds. wo is the research university: more theory, and a bachelor takes 3 years. hbo is the university of applied sciences: more practice, and a bachelor takes 4 years. Outside the Netherlands both are often called "university", so check which one a document means.

ul: vwo is the usual route to wo. havo leads to hbo. An mbo level 4 diploma also gives the right to enter hbo.

A havo diploma alone does not give access to wo. A vwo diploma or a completed hbo first year (propedeuse) gives admission to a research university. Some programmes also ask for particular subjects, and some select applicants.

Without the usual diploma, people from age 21 can usually ask for an admission test. At hbo it is called the 21+ test (toelatingsonderzoek). Research universities (wo) use a similar entrance exam without the usual diploma, called colloquium doctum, often from age 21. Some sources use both names for either kind. The institution decides and runs it, and requirements differ.
The International Baccalaureate (IB) diploma is compared with a vwo diploma. Programmes can still set subject and grade requirements, such as a maths level.

items.q: Can my child study in English at university?

blocks.p: Yes, many programmes at Dutch universities and universities of applied sciences are taught in English. Study in NL keeps a database of English-taught programmes. Entry still depends on your diploma.

A vwo diploma or a completed first year of hbo (propedeuse) gives admission to a research university, and a havo or mbo level 4 diploma gives access to hbo. Some programmes ask for particular subjects, a language test or selection. For a foreign secondary diploma, check the requirements of the programme, and ask for a Nuffic credential evaluation if the institution wants one.

groups.title: Reading the numbers on this site

items.q: How should I read the numbers on this site?

blocks.p: The numbers are context for a talk with the school, not a ranking. Pupil counts, school advice, exam results and distances come from DUO open data. To protect privacy, DUO hides groups of fewer than 5 pupils, so a blank or "fewer than 5" means the group is hidden.
Small groups also make percentages swing a lot. A school advice mix describes the pupils a school has. It does not say how good the school is.

Exam pass rates depend on who the school admits. Inspection judgements come from the Inspectie van het Onderwijs. A school without a judgement has simply not been rated yet, and that is not a bad sign.
The site never sorts schools by best.

pages.title: When must my child go to school in the Netherlands?
pages.desc: A child may start school at age 4. School is compulsory from the first day of the month after the fifth birthday, for every child who lives in the Netherlands.

pages.title: Can my child join a Dutch school without speaking Dutch?
pages.desc: Yes. In primary school newcomers can join a language class, a transition class or a regular class with extra Dutch. From age 12 there is the ISK. Ask early.

pages.title: Can my child start school mid-year in the Netherlands?
pages.desc: Yes. Children can register at any time of the year, but places can be limited, so register at more than one school. Extra support needs 10 weeks of notice.

pages.title: How the Dutch school advice works, and can you change it?
pages.desc: The school gives a school advice in group 8. The test can raise it, not lower it. A school may not place lower, but may place higher. Dates and what to ask.

pages.title: Which Dutch cities use a lottery for secondary school?
pages.desc: Amsterdam places all pupils in one central round with a random lot number. The Utrecht regions and Haaglanden draw lots at some schools. Rules change each year.

pages.title: Dutch, international or bilingual school: the difference
pages.desc: A Dutch school teaches in Dutch and charges no tuition. International schools teach in English or another language. A tto school is Dutch with English lessons.

pages.title: Can my child take the IB in the Netherlands?
pages.desc: The IB runs in the lower years (MYP) and the last two years (Diploma) at some schools. Read who can join, what it costs and where the diploma leads next.

pages.title: What do international schools in the Netherlands cost?
pages.desc: International schools charge tuition, state-funded Dutch schools do not. Rough estimate: one Amsterdam school lists 22,800 to 32,800 euro a year. Always check.

pages.title: Is Dutch school free? What is the ouderbijdrage?
pages.desc: State-funded schools charge no tuition. Many ask for a voluntary parental contribution, the ouderbijdrage. Since 2021 a school may not exclude a child over it.

pages.title: Do I need a BSN or address to register at a Dutch school?
pages.desc: You register your child yourself. Without a BSN the school can use a temporary education number from DUO. You get a BSN by registering with your municipality.

pages.title: 30% ruling and school choice in the Netherlands
pages.desc: This site gives no tax advice. Employers can sometimes pay international school fees tax-free under Belastingdienst rules. State-funded schools have no tuition.

check.title: Check with the school and your municipality
check.text: Rules and dates change every year, so check with the school and your municipality. Last checked: {date}. Facts were checked mainly against official sources (Rijksoverheid, DUO, Inspectie, Nuffic and others). Other sources, such as sector bodies and third-party guides, are labelled as such. This page was written with AI assistance. Where sources differ, the page says "usually" or "most schools".

read.title: How to read the numbers
items: DUO, the Dutch education agency, hides any count below 5 pupils to protect privacy. When you see "fewer than 5", "at least" or "partial", some small groups are missing, so the real figure is a little higher.

The numbers are context for a conversation with a school, not a ranking. A high exam pass rate or a particular school advice mix also reflects which pupils the school admits. We never sort or colour schools by quality.

An Inspectie judgement is published after an Inspectie investigation, and many schools have none because they were not investigated recently. Having a judgement, or not having one, says little by itself. Where a school has several programme judgements, we show the lowest one as a summary. That is our own rule, not an Inspectie rule, and the judgement for each programme is shown next to it.

Many schools are listed by the Inspectie without a current final judgement (Geen eindoordeel) or under basic supervision (Basistoezicht). That is not a rating and not a bad sign. We say so in words and never show it as a score.

blocks.title: What each part of a profile comes from
blocks.intro: Each block on a school profile comes from one open dataset. The periods are those of the files we used.
items: Pupils per year group and the pupil trend: DUO, pupils per location and year group, 2021-2022 to 2025-2026 (count date 1 October).

Special education (SO and VSO): DUO address file and pupils per cluster and age, 2025-2026. The type, the cluster and the pupil counts come from DUO. Support profiles and admission criteria are not open data per school and are not shown.
Reading, language and maths levels: DUO, pupils per reference level for language and maths, 2025-2026. Advice reconsidered: DUO, reconsiderations and adjusted advice, 2025-2026.
Central exam grades: DUO, exam results 2021 to 2025. Repeaters and level moves: DUO, 2024-2025 to 2025-2026.

Inspectie results and placement against the primary advice: Inspectie van het Onderwijs, onderwijsresultaten voortgezet onderwijs 2026 (CC0). Three-year averages, with the Inspectie's norms and calculated verdicts.

Inspection judgements and standards: Inspectie van het Onderwijs, open data oordelen, 1 November 2026 (CC0). The English names of the standards are our own short glosses of the Inspectie's Dutch names.

Pupils per age, per year group and level, and profile choice: DUO pupil files (age file 2025-2026, VO pupils 2021 to 2025). Pass rates per profile: DUO exam files. School exam and final list grades: DUO exam results.

about.intro: The Dutch School Guide is a free, independent guide to Dutch schools for expat and immigrant parents. It explains the school system in plain English and shows the schools near your postcode.
about.who1: The guide is made by Arktos AI Lab and run by Ernst van Gassen, an independent researcher.
about.who2: Moving to a new country is hard enough. Choosing a school when the rules and the words are in another language is harder. We wrote the guide to make that first step easier.
indep: There are no ads and no paid listings.
A school cannot pay to appear on this site or to be shown higher.
We do not rank schools. The numbers are context for a talk with a school.
The guide links to schools and to official sources. It does not replace them.
about.data1: School data comes from open government data, mainly DUO and the Inspectie van het Onderwijs. The rules and dates in the guides come from official sources where one exists, mostly the Rijksoverheid. Other sources are labelled.
about.data2: The page with the full list shows what each part of a school profile is based on.
about.ai1: The guide is built and maintained with help from AI (Claude). Each rule is tied to a source, official where one exists, and dated where it can change.
about.ai2: Mistakes are still possible. Please check details with the school and your municipality, and tell us if you find an error.
about.privH: Privacy: what the site stores and loads
priv: The site has no ads, no analytics, no tracking scripts and no accounts. It sets no cookies.

Your choices stay on your device. The site saves your language, the age and postcode you enter, your filter choices and the schools you add to compare. They are kept in your browser's local storage and are never sent to us. Clear your browser data to remove them.

The map page loads the Leaflet map code from cdnjs.cloudflare.com and map tiles from OpenStreetMap. Those services can see your IP address and the part of the map you look at, as with any web page. Nothing else loads from another site. Fonts, code and data come from this site.
The site is a set of static pages hosted on GitHub Pages. GitHub may log visits, as any web host does. We keep no visitor records ourselves.
Links to schools and official sources open other sites, with their own rules. If you write to us, we only receive what your e-mail contains.
